title: Troitsky’s Genius: Finish the Skewer
summary: Collect the queen at the end of the skewer, then coordinate the new material advantage with the h-pawn.

nodes.question: The king has left the long diagonal. Should White finish the skewer?
nodes.explanation: Qc3 attacks Qh8 through d4, e5, f6 and g7. After the illustrated ...Kf5, White can capture the queen. The complete eight-piece root is proved by that legal capture into a seven-piece exact Black loss.

branches.title: Independent continuation: let the rook take the passer
commentary: Continue independently after the source queen capture. The king and rook replies below are representative checked analysis, not moves claimed to be in the clip.
Qxh8 finishes the skewer and preserves a forced White win.
Ke6 moves Black’s king toward the center. The rook and two e-pawns remain on the board.
h6 advances White’s passer. Qh8 still occupies its promotion square, so queening will eventually require moving the queen; the pawn can also draw the rook away.
Rh4 prepares to stop the passer from behind. This is one legal defense, not an assertion that Black has no alternatives.
h7 moves the pawn next to the queen. The queen on h8 protects h7, so a rook capture can be answered.
Rxh7 removes the passer but places the rook on a square attacked by Qh8. Black still loses with best play.
Qxh7 removes the rook. White’s queen and king win against the two e-pawns in this exact ending. The h-pawn’s advance has served as a diversion rather than a completed promotion.

exercises.prompt: What makes the corner queen capturable?
exercises.answer: After ...Kf5 the black king has left Qc3’s diagonal through e5 toward h8, so Qxh8 is legal and wins the queen.

exercises.prompt: Why does advancing h7 not promote immediately?
exercises.answer: White’s own queen occupies h8. In the selected independent line the pawn instead draws Black’s rook onto h7, where Qxh7 removes it.
